answer.summary: The manuscript compares 284 self-identified ASMR experiencers, recruited via Reddit, with 279 age- and sex-matched Qualtrics panel controls who reported no tingles during a screening video. Outcomes were the MAAS (trait attentional mindfulness) and the TMS. The TMS Decentering subscale was dropped after low reliability (α=.60) and an inconsistent PCA in the ASMR group. ASMR participants scored higher on the MAAS (ηp²=.027) and on TMS Curiosity (ηp²=.023). There was a Group×Gender interaction on Curiosity, with female ASMR participants scoring higher than male ones. Within the ASMR group, mean tingle intensity correlated weakly with Curiosity (r=.16) and marginally with the MAAS (r=.11). The authors conclude that ASMR and mindfulness are related, that ASMR is a cognitively 'active' process, that the sexes may use different mechanisms, and that mindfulness training may enhance ASMR.

issues.claim: Group differences in mindfulness are confounded with recruitment source. ASMR participants came from a Reddit ASMR community, while controls came from a commercial survey panel. Sex matching was also only approximate.

evidence.exact_quote: Recruitment of participants with ASMR was conducted via an advertisement for the study
Age- and sex-matched control participants were recruited by the participant recruitment

issues.reasoning: The two groups differ in more than ASMR status: motivation, interest in introspective online communities, survey-taking habits, and attentiveness all plausibly differ between volunteer forum members and paid panel respondents. Any of these could raise MAAS and Curiosity scores. The groups also completed different procedures (controls watched a screening video; the ASMR group completed the checklist, could pause for up to two weeks, and had different numbers of questionnaires). Male proportions differ (47.5% vs 44.1%). With effect sizes of only ηp²≈.02–.03, these confounds could plausibly account for the main group differences. No covariates, attention checks, or sensitivity analyses are reported, which weakens the central claim that ASMR is related to mindfulness.

issues.claim: The TMS was used outside its validated context, with instructions modified in an unreported way. The Decentering subscale was then dropped post hoc, leaving the 'state mindfulness' comparison resting on one subscale whose meaning is unclear and whose measurement equivalence across groups was not established.

issues.reasoning: The TMS asks about experiences during a preceding meditation session. Neither the modified instructions nor the reference experience is reported, and it is unclear whether controls (who had no ASMR experience) received the same wording. If the groups rated different reference states, Curiosity scores are not comparable. The authors' own discussion suggests participants interpreted items differently (trait-like vs state). Factor structures differed between groups, yet no measurement invariance test was conducted. Dropping Decentering after inspecting the data adds analytic flexibility. Together these problems undermine the Curiosity group difference and the state/trait framing in the introduction.

issues.claim: Correlational results contain internal inconsistencies and are not corrected for multiple testing, and marginal results are interpreted as support.

The table note states N=173, yet MTotal–MAAS (.112) and MTotal–TMS-C (.160**) are identical to the values the text reports for N=284.

issues.reasoning: It is unclear which sample produced the values in Table 2, and the significance markers conflict with the text. Roughly 20 or more correlations were tested (5 factors × 2 scales, plus MTotal and additional checklist items) without correction. Several reported effects have p values between .02 and .06 (e.g., Simulations–MAAS p=.044, frisson p=.027), and these would not survive correction. Marginal results (p=.059, .055) are nonetheless interpreted as effects 'primarily due to' specific factors. This undermines the trigger-specific interpretations offered in the Discussion. It is also not explained why the factor-level analyses used only the 173 complete cases.

issues.claim: The conclusions overstate small, cross-sectional associations and make causal and mechanistic claims, including about sex differences, that the data cannot support.

issues.reasoning: Group effects explain about 2–3% of variance, and intensity correlations are r≈.11–.16, so 'strongly supports' is not warranted. Correlational data cannot show that mindfulness training would enhance ASMR, nor that ASMR is a 'cognitively active' process. The claim that males use attentional and females cognitive mechanisms rests on a Curiosity interaction with ηp²=.010 and a non-significant MAAS interaction; no measure indexes either mechanism. Table 1 also shows the Curiosity group difference lies mainly among females (15.0 vs 11.9) rather than males (13.1 vs 12.5), but group simple effects within each sex were not reported. The Discussion and Conclusions should be scaled back accordingly.

issues.claim: The TMS item-to-factor descriptions are internally inconsistent. An item presented as a Curiosity item is later listed among the 'remaining Decentering' items on a separate factor, which contradicts the statement that all Curiosity items loaded on factor 1.

issues.reasoning: Either the item is misclassified in the Methods or the PCA description is wrong. If a Curiosity item did not load with the other Curiosity items, the stated rationale for retaining the Curiosity subscale is undermined. No loading tables are provided, so readers cannot verify the factor structure or the decision to retain only Curiosity.

answer.overall_assessment: The question is novel and the samples are reasonably large, but the evidence is weaker than claimed. The main comparison confounds ASMR status with recruitment source and procedure. The TMS was adapted in unreported ways, measurement equivalence across groups was not tested, and the Decentering subscale was dropped post hoc. Effects are small, correlational analyses are uncorrected and partly inconsistent between Table 2 and the text, and marginal results are interpreted. The Discussion draws causal (mindfulness training enhances ASMR) and mechanistic (sex-specific attentional vs cognitive routes) conclusions that the data do not support. Substantial revision is needed: report full TMS instructions and loadings, test invariance, address sampling confounds, correct the inconsistencies, adjust for multiplicity, and temper the conclusions.
